title: Size and Impurity Effects on Scattering of Valley Hall Modes in Gate-Defined Bilayer Graphene Superlattices
authors: Marcus N. Kanestrøm, Antonio L. R. Manesco, D. O. Oriekhov
abstract: In the present paper we perform a tight-binding simulation of gate-defined islands in Bernal bilayer graphene (BLG). The inversion of the gap sign on the boundaries of the islands creates topologically-protected valley Hall modes. We focus on the specific questions of whether the valley Hall modes around such islands could serve as a host for quantum walks or simulate weakly coupled systems, and how their tunneling is affected by in-gap impurities. In addition, we discuss the effect of misalignment of top and bottom gate patterns on the tunneling properties between islands. Our main results show that resonant tunneling via an impurity enhances overlap between superlattice islands, while misalignment does not break topological protection over a wide parameter regime. In addition, we study the two-island geometry and show that it is possible to leverage suppressed scattering to place islands more densely on a single sample.
summary: This work simulates the behavior of topologically-protected valley Hall modes in patterned bilayer graphene superlattices. Using tight-binding methods, the authors show that impurities can facilitate resonant tunneling between islands, while the topological protection remains robust against certain device imperfections. This research advances the understanding of engineered topological quantum transport in 2D materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates the scattering properties of topologically-protected valley Hall modes in engineered bilayer graphene superlattices.
main_result: Resonant tunneling via impurities enhances island overlap, and the topological protection remains robust even with misalignment of gate patterns.
method: The study employs tight-binding simulations and analyzes the scattering matrix (S-matrix) to probe quantum transport phenomena.
model_or_system: The system is Bernal bilayer graphene (BLG) patterned into superlattices using gate-defined islands, creating a sign-alternating gap structure that hosts valley Hall modes.
key_observables: Scattering probability, resonant tunneling enhancement, and the persistence of topological protection.
important_parameters: Interlayer bias ($U_0$), impurity potential strength, and the separation distance ($L$) between superlattice islands.
main_assumptions: The model assumes the ability to engineer a device with an alternating gap structure and treats the system using a spinless, nearest-neighbor tight-binding Hamiltonian.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device setup, the VHM profile near domain walls, and energy sweeps showing oscillatory tunneling effects dependent on island separation.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using a tight-binding Hamiltonian, then analyzes the existence of topologically-protected valley Hall modes, and finally investigates how impurity scattering and island geometry affect these modes.
why_interesting: The study directly models topological edge states and their interaction with disorder (impurities), which is highly relevant for understanding robust quantum transport in mesoscopic systems.

FIG. 3. The transverse VHM profile along the electrostatic domain wall for each of the two helical modes present on either side. The electrostatic domain wall is denoted by the vertical red dashed line. What we see is that due to the unequal A and B lattice sites on either side of the domain wall, the wavefunction has two peaks on the inside and outside.

FIG. 4. The evanescent decay lengths of the VHM for various interlayer biases and smoothening parameters. To make the domain wall sign shift more like a step-function, a smaller smoothening parameter (Ismooth) is chosen. Whereas a larger smoothening parameter indicates a longer bias sign transition. We see that for small interlayer biases (on the top row), we get larger decay lengths ζ(a). Additionally, for larger Ismooth, we get a longer decay length which is seen on the bottom row. ∆ζ is the difference in decay length units (a) between the chosen smoothening parameter and Ismooth = 1.
